clue.text: Anger badly out of place, on the whole

indicators.note: letters that are out of place are not where they belong, so the two words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone notes that temper shown at the wrong moment is, in general, a bad thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder: ANGER and BADLY together give the ten letters, and 'out of place' tells you to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean generally, taking everything into account.

clue.text: One may be out without this security

definitions.text: One may be out without this security

parts.words: One may be out without this security
parts.note: a prisoner can be released from custody against a money guarantee, though some are freed without one

explanation.surface: A remark that one might be released without a guarantee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' suggests a dismissed batsman, but it is a person let out of custody before trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Money pledged to secure a suspect's release is a form of security.

clue.text: A flower for Florence

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river, and this one runs through Florence

explanation.surface: A bloom presented to a woman named Florence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is the crossword's flow-er, a river, and Florence is the Italian city, not a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The river that flows through the Tuscan city of Florence.

clue.text: Emily craved a change, being reckless

indicators.note: a change of arrangement signals that these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Emily wanted something different and became wild.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who doesn't care what happens is carefree to the point of rashness.

clue.text: How players behaved

parts.note: players are actors, and what actors did on stage is perform; behaved also means performed

explanation.surface: A question about the conduct of a sports team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'players' suggests a sports team, but they are stage actors, and 'behaved' covers both conduct and performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Players on stage performed, and to behave is also to comport oneself.

clue.text: "Then I'll give o'er, And bid the world —" (Herrick)

definitions.text: "Then I'll give o'er, And bid the world —" (Herrick)

parts.words: "Then I'll give o'er, And bid the world —" (Herrick)
parts.note: a quotation from the poet Robert Herrick with its closing words, a farewell, left blank

explanation.surface: A line of Herrick with its last words missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the blank in Herrick's line, a farewell bidding the world a nightly goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell said at bedtime completes the poet's line about leaving the world.

clue.text: Captured Alexandrian ?

explanation.surface: A man from Alexandria has been taken prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Copt' is an old past tense of cop, to seize; and a Copt is an Egyptian Christian, whose church is centred on Alexandria.

clue.text: A dead man? Never.

parts.note: from the song saying veterans of the army never die but only fade away

explanation.surface: A denial that someone has died.
explanation.walkthrough: The barrack-room song runs 'Old soldiers never die, they only fade away'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song claims army veterans never die, so such a man is never dead.

clue.text: Come across the lines?

parts.note: to go across, trans-, the lines of a poem, verse; or simply to lie crosswise

explanation.surface: An invitation to cross over the boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: The word splits as TRANS (across) and VERSE (lines of poetry); as an old verb it means to cross.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lying crosswise runs across, as a crossing line does.

clue.text: Something new in public acclaim ?

parts.note: a public house, a pub, is an inn
an ovation is a burst of applause, public acclaim

explanation.surface: A novelty is greeted with applause from the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'public' is short for public house, so it gives INN; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A novelty or fresh idea is a new departure, something introduced for the first time.

clue.text: Make a further note to return these old books

indicators.note: returning means the whole run of letters built so far is read backwards

parts.note: to make a further amount is to add
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: An instruction to annotate some ancient volumes before sending them back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' turns ADD followed by E backwards. The Edda is the collection of Old Norse poems and prose, so 'these old books' fits.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eddas are medieval Icelandic compilations of Norse myth and poetry, ancient volumes.

clue.text: Also how one puts two and two together ?

definitions.text: how one puts two and two together

explanation.surface: A note on reaching an obvious conclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: Putting two and two together, read literally, is done by adding, so it is done additionally: by addition.
explanation.definitionFit: Also means in addition; and combining two and two is done by addition.

clue.text: Open-and-shut affairs in a single plane

definitions.text: Open-and-shut affairs in a single plane

parts.words: Open-and-shut affairs in a single plane
parts.note: things that open and close by moving flat along one plane rather than swinging on hinges

explanation.surface: Simple cases, all handled on the same level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open-and-shut' usually means obvious, as of a legal case; here it is literal, things that open and shut, and 'plane' is a flat surface, not an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: Panels that run along a track slide open and shut without leaving their flat plane.

clue.text: They're asking for it, with a very soft tyro in charge of the workers

parts.note: PP, pianissimo, is the musical mark for very soft
a tyro is a learner, L
ants are the stock crossword workers

explanation.surface: They deserve trouble, those with a feeble beginner put over the staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'asking for it' suggests deserving trouble, but it means people making a request.
explanation.definitionFit: Candidates for a post are requesting it, making an application.

clue.text: Shakespeare's duke makes much 'of the king-of-arms

annotationWithheld.why: Shakespeare's duke makes much of the king-of-arms (10): CLARENCE is the duke, but no clue word gives the final UX; 'makes much of' only says the duke is most of the answer.
annotationWithheld.clue: Shakespeare's duke makes much 'of the king-of-arms

clue.text: Beating the signal put out in code' ?

indicators.note: a message put out in code has its letters scrambled, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Thrashing the opponent depends on a coded signal being sent.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart that is throbbing rhythmically is pulsing or beating.

clue.text: No decline, anyhow, in laziness

indicators.note: anyhow means in any old way, so the letters of No decline are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A slothful person turns down nothing, whatever happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Idleness and sloth are synonyms for laziness.

clue.text: Somewhere in France to find relatively easily

indicators.note: the answer can be found easily because it sits in plain view across the words find relatively

explanation.surface: A place in France that is relatively easy to locate.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across 'fIND RElatively'. Indre is a river and a department in central France.
explanation.definitionFit: Indre is a French department named after its river, so it is a place in France.

clue.text: Poem that took a brief year in '51, about

indicators.note: one piece took the other, holding it inside

parts.note: LI is 51 in Roman numerals
YR is the short form of year
C, circa, is Latin for about

explanation.surface: A verse composition that was a year or so in the making, back in 1951.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in '51 marks an abbreviated year, but the number is read as a Roman numeral; 'took' is the container signal, and 'about' is the Latin circa.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyric is a short poem expressing personal feeling, often meant to be sung.

clue.text: Prisoners need a site for recreation

indicators.note: re-creation means making again, so the letters before are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Inmates require somewhere to exercise and relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recreation' reads as leisure for the prisoners, but it is re-creation, the signal to rearrange NEED A SITE.
explanation.definitionFit: People held in custody are prisoners.

clue.text: Middling concentration brings us to the point

explanation.surface: Paying moderate attention eventually gets us to what matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing things into the middle is a concentration at the centre; and making something central draws it to a single point.

clue.text: Head first into battle.

parts.note: a weapon that is thrust or thrown point-first at the enemy goes in head first

explanation.surface: A command to charge recklessly into the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head first' suggests a reckless charge, but a spear has a head and it leads into the fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A spear has a pointed head that strikes first in combat.

clue.text: One room for boffins up in the island. .

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the pieces are read from bottom to top

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
boffins are scientists, and their room is a laboratory, a lab

explanation.surface: A single room for scientists set up on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns I followed by LAB backwards. 'Boffins' is British slang for scientists.
explanation.definitionFit: Bali is an Indonesian island.

clue.text: … and Boffin's wooden-legged old rascal, Silas

definitions.text: and Boffin's wooden-legged old rascal, Silas

parts.words: and Boffin's wooden-legged old rascal, Silas
parts.note: the one-legged ballad-seller who schemes against Mr Boffin in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend

explanation.surface: A follow-on clue naming a peg-legged villain from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: After 22, 'Boffin' turns from scientist to Mr Boffin, the Golden Dustman of Our Mutual Friend, whom Silas Wegg tries to blackmail.
explanation.definitionFit: Silas Wegg is the wooden-legged rogue in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend.

clue.text: "Man proposes …" but if these have it he's lost

definitions.text: "Man proposes …" but if these have it he's lost

parts.words: "Man proposes …" but if these have it he's lost
parts.note: a proposer in debate, or a suitor proposing marriage, loses when the votes or replies against him carry the day

explanation.surface: The proverb that man proposes, God disposes, applied to a doomed suitor.
explanation.walkthrough: In Parliament the Speaker announces 'the ayes have it' or 'the noes have it'; if the votes against carry, the man who proposed the motion is defeated.
explanation.definitionFit: Votes or replies against a proposal defeat whoever made it.

clue.text: Put in the paper Mark Antony's objective

explanation.surface: A newspaper item about the aims of Caesar's friend.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Antony says 'I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him': his aim is to inter Caesar and leave him there, read as INTER + LEAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To insert blank sheets between the pages of a book is to put paper in; and to bury and then walk away is what Antony claims to intend.

clue.text: Blue bags, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the word for bags is pronounced, not written

parts.note: bags are sacks

explanation.surface: A question of whether some luggage could be called blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Saxe blue is a light greyish blue, named after Saxony.
explanation.definitionFit: Saxe is a pale greyish-blue colour.

clue.text: Buttons in such royal guise could have gone to the ball

definitions.text: Buttons in such royal guise could have gone to the ball

parts.words: Buttons in such royal guise could have gone to the ball
parts.note: Buttons, the servant in the Cinderella pantomime, dressed as a costermonger monarch whose suit is covered in buttons

explanation.surface: The pantomime servant, dressed up as a king, might have joined Cinderella at the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: Buttons is Cinderella's friend in British pantomime. A pearly king is a London street-trader 'monarch' whose clothes are sewn all over with pearl buttons.
explanation.definitionFit: Costermonger royalty in London wear outfits covered in mother-of-pearl buttons, a regal disguise of sorts.
